observation: Transaction throughput is critically affected by the order in which conflicting transactions execute, yet practical systems generally process transactions in FIFO order and resolve conflicts reactively, and recent scheduling techniques explore only a small subset of possible schedules. The resulting performance gap is large and systematic: for a batch of four conflicting transactions one schedule can reduce makespan by 25% over another, the gap grows arbitrarily for larger workloads, and on real workload traces FIFO can increase makespan over optimized schedules by 43.2% for Epinions, 8.0% for SmallBank, 96.2% for TAOBench, 101.6% for TPC-C, and 99.3% for YCSB. Finding an optimal schedule is NP-complete, and existing heuristics sacrifice schedule quality for efficiency.

claims: Most existing concurrency control protocols execute requests based on arrival-FIFO-order and handle conflicting operations only after they have arrived or executed, missing opportunities to avoid conflicts by planning ahead.
Most concurrency-control techniques operate within the implicit constraint of arrival order and deal with conflicts as they appear.
Existing techniques that address the schedule explicitly do so only by assigning a schedule based on arrival order or by reordering the schedule after transaction commit and/or abort.

claims: Recent work schedules transactions more intelligently by using full read-write access sets in deterministic databases or predicted key accesses, but for efficiency considers only a small subset of the schedule space such as partitioning workloads on hot keys or randomly deferring requests, resulting in suboptimal decisions.
Deterministic databases schedule batches of requests explicitly; many use FIFO order, while some improve schedules by partitioning workloads based on hot keys.
More recent scheduling proposals predict hot keys and probabilistically delay requests, or learn abort patterns, instead of systematically searching the schedule space.

claims: MVTSO assigns each transaction a unique timestamp corresponding to its serialization order, exposes uncommitted writes, and aborts transactions whose writes would violate the order of earlier reads.
MVTSO assigns timestamps in arrival order and does not delay later-scheduled transactions from executing before earlier ones, causing unnecessary aborts even though it enables high concurrency.
MVTSO imposes minimal execution constraints to ensure serializability compared with pessimistic locking such as two-phase locking.

claims: Transaction scheduling can be framed as an instance of the well-known job-shop scheduling problem, which has a large corpus of solution techniques.
Exact job-shop optimization methods rely on full enumeration and can be applied only to small problems, while approximation methods are used for larger problems.

Job-shop approximation methods include construction heuristics such as NEH, iterative approaches such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search, and hybrid methods, and recent work also applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to job-shop scheduling.
Modeling transaction scheduling as job-shop scheduling requires accounting for read and write operation types and for sequence-dependent execution requirements studied in some job-shop problems.

solution.idea: The core idea is to make the transaction schedule an explicit search target rather than an incidental side effect of arrival order. Observing that makespan is increased by conflict costs and that optimal scheduling is NP-complete, SMF greedily builds a schedule by repeatedly appending the unscheduled transaction whose addition produces the smallest incremental makespan. To keep search tractable and deployable online, SMF makes decisions from predicted hot-key conflict patterns instead of full read/write sets, relies on a small random sample of candidates, and computes only the incremental cost of the latest conflicting operation per hot key; focusing on hot keys preserves most of the scheduling benefit because hot-key conflicts dominate makespan. Once a low-makespan schedule is found, a schedule-first MVTSO-derived protocol, MVSchedO, enforces the selected order only for hot keys, delaying later conflicting operations until earlier ones complete, thereby avoiding the aborts and race conditions that would otherwise undo the schedule's benefit.
solution.implementation:
R-SMF has three main components: a classifier, an SMF scheduler, and the MVSchedO protocol. Applications annotate the START statement with a transaction-type id and a set of hot key names (or other metadata). The classifier is trained on transaction traces: each transaction is converted into an integer metadata vector; clustering is run over training vectors using Euclidean distance; the number of clusters k is chosen by validation error; and each cluster is assigned the canonical set of hot key operations, i.e., the operation type and position that occurs most frequently among its transactions. At runtime a KNN classifier maps the hints of a new transaction to a cluster and returns its canonical predicted hot-key operation set.

The SMF scheduler works online over in-flight transactions. It seeds the schedule with a random transaction, then repeatedly samples s=5 unscheduled transactions uniformly at random, computes for each candidate the incremental makespan that would result from appending it to the current schedule using the predicted hot-key operations and the makespan model from Section 2.1 (operations take unit time, conflicting operations are serialized, transactions have internal operation order), and appends the candidate with the smallest increase, breaking ties randomly. Transactions with no predicted hot keys are assumed not to affect makespan and execute immediately. For each hot key, only the latest transaction's conflicting operation is retained when computing costs because earlier conflicts were already accounted for when that transaction was added to the schedule. Barriers in the scheduling queues prevent starvation. The scheduler has O(n*s) runtime for n in-flight transactions and s sampled candidates. Optionally, schedule quality can be checked in the background by uniformly sampling schedules using the acyclic-orientation random walk and one-sided tolerance intervals; if SMF's makespan deviates significantly, the system can fall back to FIFO.

MVSchedO starts from MVTSO. SMF assigns each transaction a unique timestamp and serialization order at START_TXN. For each predicted hot key operation, PREDICT_HOT_KEY_OPS inserts the operation into pred_ops for that key. When a transaction executes READ_KEY or WRITE_KEY on a key in hot_keys, the operation first invokes SCHED_KEY, which waits until the minimum timestamp among not-yet-executed predicted operations on that key is at least the transaction's timestamp, meaning all predicted earlier conflicting operations on the key have executed. It then performs the ordinary MVTSO read or write and removes its predicted operation from pred_ops. If a predicted hot key access never occurs, no deadlock occurs because COMMIT or abort calls FREE_HOT_KEY_DEPS to remove the transaction's remaining predicted operations before MVTSO commit validation. All other MVTSO mechanisms, including commit checks and write-dependency tracking, remain unchanged. Since MVTSO timestamp assignment is arbitrary and MVSchedO only delays operations that could otherwise execute under MVTSO, serializability is preserved; MVSchedO executes a schedule with the maximum concurrency permitted under the schedule.

In the R-SMF system, these components are integrated into RocksDB's transaction manager: START accepts hints, runs the classifier, SMF may queue the transaction until it is scheduled, and scheduled transactions register predicted hot-key operations with MVSchedO. A bolt-on variant starts transactions according to SMF but lets the original OCC, Lock, or TAO protocol execute them without further operation-level control; this also gives substantial gains, though smaller than using MVSchedO.
